title: Common intention vs common object - a frequently confused distinction
p1:
Two people can participate in the same crime without having the same intention.

Sounds confusing? This is exactly where many people mix up common intention and common object.
p2:
The biggest misconception is that both terms mean the same thing. They don't.

Common intention means two or more people share a plan and act together to carry it out. There must be a shared intention, along with participation in furthering that plan.

Common object, on the other hand, relates to an unlawful assembly of five or more people sharing a common purpose. Every member need not have the same personal intention or actively participate in every act.
p3:
Here's a simple way to remember the difference:

Common intention = Shared plan and coordinated action.

Common object = Shared purpose of an unlawful assembly, with liability arising under specific legal conditions.

Here's the surprising part: Under common object, a member may be held responsible for an offence committed by another member if the statutory requirements are satisfied, even without proof of an identical intention.

The distinction is not just about terminology. It can significantly affect criminal liability.

Note: Under Indian law, these concepts are covered by Sections 3(5) and 190 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, respectively.
conclusion: What do you think is the most commonly misunderstood difference between common intention and common object? Share your understanding in the comments.
